newsitem.title: JAPAN: Former Nomura chief indicted in racketeer scandal.
newsitem.headline: Former Nomura chief indicted in racketeer scandal.

text.p: Tokyo prosecutors on Thursday charged former Nomura Securities president Hideo Sakamaki with making illegal payoffs to a racketeer as worries persisted that Japan's high-profile financial scandal could spread further.

Prosecutors charged that Sakamaki, who resigned over the scandal after it broke in March, had paid 49.73 million yen ($440,000) to "sokaiya" racketeer Ryuichi Koike between January 31 and June 15, 1995.

They also served Sakamaki and two other former Nomura executives with new warrants alleging they conspired to pay Koike 320 million yen ($2.83 million) in cash around March 24, 1995, in exchange for a pledge by him to ensure that the firm's June shareholders meeting went without a hitch.
Nomura said it was shocked by the fresh allegations.
"If the suspicion is true, we would have to say we would be stunned," the brokerage said in a one-sentence statement.
Payoffs to sokaiya, who extort money by threatening to disrupt shareholders meetings, have been illegal since 1982 but firms have found it tough to cut their ties to the underworld.
The affair has already led to more than a dozen arrests including executives from Nomura and one of Japan's biggest banks, Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd.
Nomura -- now entangled in its second scandal in six years -- has been indicted for illegally compensating a company owned by Koike's brother for trading losses.
Two former Nomura directors have been indicted on charges of paying off Koike, who has been arrested as have 10 officials from DKB.

The scandal is unfolding just as Japan kicks off its "Big Bang" reforms of its stodgy financial sector, a coincidence which has made authorities -- including Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto -- keen to be seen taking a stern stance.

"Obviously, it is very important for the finance ministry to establish clearly that certain things are right and certain things are wrong as they move into a deregulated environment," said Alicia Ogawa, financial analyst at Salomon Brothers Asia.
Sakamaki's indictment could pave the way for financial authorities to decide what penalties to impose on the brokerage, though uncertainties remain over whether more arrests are in store.

In addition, no formal decision is likely while Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka is out of town. He will attend the summit of Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations from June 20-22 and will then visit China before returning to Tokyo on June 27.
Nomura, already suffering from client defections and suspended from underwriting government-backed bonds, could be ordered to halt some of its business for up to six months.
But whether the penalties will include banning the brokerage from dealing securities on its own account for the full six months allowed by law remains to be seen.
Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank is also suffering from the scandal.

Deposits have shrunk, the Finance Ministry has suspended the bank from Japanese government bond (JGB) auctions and JGB underwriting "for the time being," and some local governments are taking similar steps.
The ministry said that if a complaint were filed with prosecutors against the bank, the suspension would remain in place until subsequent administrative penalties were imposed.

Nomura and DKB aside, fears that other financial institutions will be dragged into the scandal were fanned this week after an opposition lawmaker made public DKB documents showing that 17 brokerages had transferred 1.72 billion yen ($15.2 million) to accounts held at the bank by Koike.

"The danger is that more and more companies will come under suspicion," said Brian Waterhouse, financial analyst at HSCB James Capel. "That would be bad for the stock market and do nothing to increase confidence in the securities industry or the clarity of authorities' supervision."
Whether the scandal saga takes a political twist also remains unclear.

Media reports have said prosecutors were seeking evidence of possible misdeeds in connection with some 8,000-9,000 "VIP" accounts set up at Nomura for elite customers including politicians and bureaucrats.
Nomura has denied the accounts were designed to give illegal preferential treatment.
Some experts said chances the affair would spread beyond the two blue-chip financial firms were actually dwindling.
"If history is any guide, if it were going to spread, it would have spread more quickly," said one foreign analyst.
